transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I suppose... I suppose I'm here because I just don't know what else to do at this point. You see, I’ve always been the organized one. In my career, and even in retirement, I was always the man with the lists and the plan. I had a schedule for everything, kept the whole house running like clockwork. 

But recently... well, my wife had a terrible fall. It was awful, just out of nowhere, and ever since she came home, I just... I've completely fallen apart. I mean, I literally just sit at the kitchen table for hours. I’ll just sit there, staring at her medication chart, trying to figure out what she needs next, and I just can't seem to process it. And my emotions are just all over the place—I’ll start crying over absolutely nothing, or I’ll find myself snapping at her, which isn't like me at all. I've never been a short-tempered man, but the slightest thing sets me off now. 

And everything else is just... it's just piling up. The bills are sitting there on the counter, completely unopened. I usually do these mentoring calls for young folks starting out in my old field, and I haven't returned a single message. I just let them pile up. Even just the basic housework... the dishes are stacked high in the sink, the laundry is sitting in baskets... it’s all just piling up around us. It’s like I just can’t make myself function anymore. I sit there and tell myself to get up and do it, and I just... I can't. I just can't.
How long have you been feeling this way since your wife's fall?

Well, let's see... the fall happened on a Tuesday, I remember because it was the day the street sweepers come, and I had just moved the car. And then there was the hospital stay, which was a nightmare in itself, and then the rehab center... but really, this feeling, this complete inability to cope with everything, it's been going on for about two months now. Yes, right around two months. 

It started the day they finally discharged her and brought her back to the house. I thought I had everything ready, you know? I had moved the rugs, installed the grab bars in the bathroom—which, by the way, took three trips to the hardware store because the first set didn't have the right anchors for our tile—but the moment the medical transport van pulled away and it was just the two of us... that's when it hit me. That was two months ago. Two months of just... sitting at that table, watching the mail pile up, watching the dust gather on the mantelpiece. 

I keep thinking, "Tomorrow, I'll open those bills," or "Tomorrow, I'll call David back about his career advice," but then tomorrow comes, and it's just exactly the same. Two whole months of this. It feels like a lifetime, to be honest with you. Before that, everything was fine. Everything was perfectly fine and ordered. But these last two months... it's like I'm a completely different person living in my own house.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like before your wife's fall?

Well, enjoyment... that's a strong word these days. I used to love working in the garden, you know. We have this beautiful rose bush out back, a David Austin variety, absolutely stunning apricot color. I planted it right after I retired, spent hours making sure the soil pH was just right, pruning it, keeping the aphids away with this organic spray I mix up myself. It was my pride and joy, my little sanctuary. I would go out there every morning with my coffee, just looking at the blooms, planning out what I was going to do with the side beds...

But now? Now I look out the kitchen window at it, and I just... I don't feel anything. I can see the weeds creeping up around the base, I can see that it needs deadheading, and I just don't care. It's the same with my woodworking. I have a whole shop set up in the garage—lathe, bandsaw, everything. I was right in the middle of making a set of nesting tables for our daughter. Beautiful cherry wood, I had just finished sanding the tops to a 400-grit finish, smooth as glass. But since she came home... I haven't even turned on the lights out there. The sawdust is just settling on everything. 

I try to tell myself I should go out there, that it would be good for me, take my mind off things. But the thought of actually doing it, of actually trying to find joy in it... it just feels impossible. It's like all the color has just been drained out of everything I used to love. Even reading—I used to tear through historical biographies, loved them—but now I read the same paragraph five times and I couldn't tell you a single word of it. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm enjoying anything at all right now. It's just... it's all just flat.
Do you feel guilty about not being able to care for your wife or manage the household as you used to?

Guilty? Oh... oh, doctor, you have no idea. The guilt is... it's just eating me alive, to be perfectly honest with you. It's like this heavy, lead weight sitting right in the center of my chest, from the moment I wake up until I finally manage to fall asleep. 

You see, I took my vows very seriously. "In sickness and in health," right? I always pictured myself being the strong one, the one who would take care of her if anything ever happened. We've been married for forty-two years this coming October—we actually got married in this beautiful little chapel up in the mountains, it was raining that day, pouring actually, but they say that's good luck—and for all those forty-two years, I was the provider. I was the one who fixed things when they broke, the one who managed the finances, the one who made sure the cars had their oil changed every three thousand miles on the dot. 

And now... now I look at her sitting in that recliner in the living room, the one we bought specifically because it has the power lift feature to help her stand up, and I just feel this overwhelming sense of failure. She asks me for a glass of water, and I'll get up to get it, but I'll stand in the kitchen staring at the glasses in the cupboard, and I just start crying. Over a glass of water! And she sees it. She sees me falling apart. I'm supposed to be her rock right now, I'm supposed to be the one keeping everything together, and instead, I'm the one having a breakdown over the laundry basket. 

I look at the bills on the counter, and I know they need paying. I know there's a system, I built the system! I have a whole filing cabinet organized alphabetically and chronologically, color-coded folders and everything. But I just can't bring myself to open the envelopes. And then I feel guilty about that, because what if they shut off the electricity? What if we lose the house because I couldn't bring myself to write a simple check? The guilt is just... it's paralyzing. It's absolutely paralyzing. I feel like I'm letting her down in the most profound way possible, right when she needs me the absolute most. It's just awful. It's just truly awful.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight since your wife's fall?

Weight? Oh, well, I... I haven't really been paying attention to the scale, to be honest. I mean, I used to step on it every Sunday morning, right after my shower, before breakfast. It was a whole routine. I'd log it in this little notebook I kept in the top drawer of the vanity, just to make sure I was staying within a healthy range, especially after my doctor mentioned my blood pressure a few years back. But since... since she came home, I haven't even looked at that scale. It's just sitting there gathering dust, like everything else in the house.

I suppose my clothes might be fitting a bit differently, but I've mostly just been wearing these loose sweatpants and old t-shirts around the house. There's no reason to put on a belt or a proper pair of trousers when you're just sitting at the kitchen table all day, staring at the wall. So, no, I haven't noticed any specific changes in my weight. I couldn't give you a number. My appetite is completely shot, of course. I used to make us these wonderful breakfasts—eggs over easy, whole wheat toast, a little bit of fresh fruit on the side—but now I just force down a piece of dry toast if I remember to eat at all. But as for actual weight lost or gained? I really couldn't say. I just haven't been keeping track of those sorts of things anymore. It all just seems so trivial compared to everything else that's going wrong.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live or harming yourself since your wife's fall?

Harming myself? Oh, no... no, doctor. Goodness, no. I mean, I know I've been sitting here telling you how miserable everything is, how I can't eat, how I can't bring myself to even look at the mail or go out to my woodshop... and I know it sounds bleak. It *is* bleak, I won't lie to you about that. The days just stretch on forever, and the nights are even worse, just lying there listening to the clock tick in the hallway. It's a grandfather clock, an antique we bought at an estate sale back in 1985, beautiful mahogany case, chimes every quarter hour. I used to love the sound of it, found it so comforting, but now every chime just reminds me of how much time is passing while we're stuck in this... this nightmare. 

But as for actually ending it all? Or hurting myself? No. I couldn't do that. I could never do that. I mean, think about it... if I were gone, who would take care of her? I know I'm doing a terrible job of it right now, I know I'm crying over water glasses and letting the bills pile up, but I'm still physically here. I'm still the one who helps her get out of that recliner, the one who makes sure her walker is positioned right so she doesn't trip on the rug. We have this Persian rug in the living room, hand-knotted, we brought it back from a trip to Turkey years ago... the edges curl up just a bit, and I'm always terrified she's going to catch her foot on it. If I weren't here, who would watch out for that? 

Our daughter, Sarah, she lives three states away. She has her own life, her own career—she's a senior partner at a law firm, works eighty hours a week, bless her heart. I can't leave this mess for her to clean up. I can't leave my wife alone. So, no matter how heavy that weight in my chest gets, no matter how much I just want to pull the covers over my head and never come out... I'm not going to do anything like that. I don't want to die. I just... I just want things to go back to how they were before she fell. I want my life back. But I'm not going to take my own life, no. I promise you that.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body, watching yourself sitting at the kitchen table, or like you're in a dream and nothing feels real?

Outside of my body? Like... like watching myself? No, no, I can't say that I do. I mean, I wish I did, to be perfectly honest with you. If this all felt like a dream, well, then there would be a chance I might wake up from it, wouldn't there? But no, it doesn't feel like a dream at all. It feels... it feels entirely, crushingly real. 

When I'm sitting at that kitchen table—it's a solid oak table, Amish-made, we actually drove all the way out to Pennsylvania to pick it up ourselves back in '98, strapped it right to the roof of the station wagon we had back then—when I'm sitting there, I am very much in my own body. I feel every bit of that heavy weight in my chest I was telling you about. I just sit there and stare at the grain of the wood. I know every knot and swirl in that table. I can see where the varnish is starting to wear thin on the edge where she usually sits, right by the window where the morning light comes in. 

I'm not floating above it or anything like that. I'm just glued to the chair. And everything around me is just so sharply in focus, you know? The stack of mail next to the napkin holder, the sound of the refrigerator... it's a Whirlpool, it's about fifteen years old now, and the compressor has started making this awful rattling sound every time it kicks on. I should really pull it out and vacuum the coils, maybe check the fan motor, but I just sit there listening to it rattle. It's all just so real. The silence in the house, the ticking of that grandfather clock I mentioned, the rattling of the fridge... it's not a dream at all. I'm stuck right here in the middle of it, in this body, and I can't escape it for a single second. So, no, doctor, I don't feel disconnected like that. I feel far too connected to the reality of it all, if anything.
Do you often feel restless or have trouble relaxing when you're not sitting at the kitchen table?

Restless? Trouble relaxing? Well, I... I suppose you could say that, but it's not like a physical pacing around the room kind of restlessness. It's more of an internal thing. When I'm not at the kitchen table—which, as I said, is where I spend the vast majority of my time these days—I'm usually just moving from one room to another without any real purpose. I'll get up because my back starts to ache from sitting in that wooden chair for so long, and I'll wander into the living room. 

I'll stand there and look at her recliner. It's one of those power lift chairs, you know, the ones that tilt forward to help you stand up? We bought it a few years ago when her arthritis started getting really bad in her knees. It's a dark brown leather, very plush, very comfortable, but now it just looks like this... this medical device sitting right in the middle of our living room. And I'll stand there looking at it, and I'll think, "I should sit down on the sofa and read a book." I have a whole stack of biographies I've been meaning to get to—I've always been a big history buff, especially the Civil War era—but I can't bring myself to even pick one up. 

If I do sit on the sofa, I'm just perched on the edge of the cushion. I can't sink into it. I can't lean back and put my feet up on the coffee table like I used to. It's a glass-top coffee table with a brass frame, and I'm always so careful not to scratch it, but now I don't even care. I just sit on the edge, and my mind is racing. I'm thinking about the rug, the stairs, the bathroom tiles... every surface in the house feels like a hazard now. I'm listening for her breathing if she's asleep, or waiting for her to call out for me. 

So, relaxing? No. I don't think I've relaxed for a single second since she fell. Even when I'm lying in bed at night, staring at the ceiling, my muscles are tense. My shoulders are practically up around my ears all the time. I tried taking a hot bath the other night, thinking maybe the warm water would loosen me up. We have a nice deep soaking tub in the master bath, cast iron, holds the heat wonderfully. But I just sat in the water, staring at the faucet, listening to it drip... drip... drip. It needs a new washer, I know it does, it's a simple fix, but I couldn't even bring myself to care about fixing it. I just sat there, completely rigid, until the water went cold. So, yes, I suppose I am restless, but it's a very... paralyzing kind of restlessness, if that makes any sense.
Do you often feel overwhelmed by worry or fear about your wife's health or your ability to care for her?

Overwhelmed? Oh, doctor... overwhelmed doesn't even begin to cover it. Honestly, that right there is exactly why I came in to see you. It's the fear, this constant, gnawing fear that I'm going to do something wrong, that I'm failing her. Because... well, you have to understand, before she took that terrible tumble down those three little steps by the garage—I’ve always been the organized one. I spent my career in administration, so my whole life, I was always the man with the lists and the plan. I had spreadsheets for everything, schedules for house maintenance, our finances, our travel... everything was orderly and handled. I always knew exactly what to do next.

But since my wife’s fall? I've gone from being that man to... to just a complete wreck. I sit at that same oak kitchen table I was telling you about, and I just stare at her medication chart. The hospital discharge nurse made it for us, it's color-coded, pink for morning, blue for evening, detailing her blood thinners and the painkillers... and I just sit there and stare at it until the words blur together. And then I start crying. Just sitting there sobbing over a piece of paper. Or, God forgive me, I end up snapping at her over absolutely nothing—she'll just ask for a glass of water or ask what time it is, and I bite her head off. I don't mean to, I really don't, it's just the pressure of it all boiling over. 

And the rest of my life is just crumbling while I worry about her. I'm letting the bills pile up in that stack next to the napkin holder. I used to do this alumni mentoring program for my old university, you know, helping recent grads figure out their career paths, but I've completely abandoned it. I let all those mentoring calls go straight to voicemail, I can't even bear to look at the phone when it rings. Even the basic housework... the dust is gathering on the baseboards, the laundry is sitting in baskets, and I just look at it and let it pile up. It's like... it's like I just can’t make myself function anymore. The worry about her health, about whether I'm actually capable of keeping her safe and doing this right... it's completely paralyzed me. I just don't know how to be the man with the plan anymore.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain tasks or activities because they remind you of your wife's condition or your current situation?

Avoiding tasks because they remind me of it? No... no, I wouldn't say that's it at all. I mean, how could I possibly avoid a reminder, doctor? The entire house is a reminder. There is no escaping it. The color-coded medication chart is right there on the Amish oak table, that power lift chair is dominating the living room, her walker is parked right by the hallway... the reality of her condition is staring me in the face twenty-four hours a day. I couldn't avoid being reminded of it even if I blindfolded myself. 

I am avoiding things, certainly. I haven't been doing the grocery shopping, for instance. I've been having the neighbor boy across the street do it for us. Well, I call him a boy, he's a young man now really, just finished his freshman year at the state college, studying civil engineering I believe, a very bright kid, always very polite. Anyway, I've been giving him a list and some cash to pick up our essentials at the Stop & Shop over on Route 9. But I don't avoid going to the store because the store reminds me of my wife or her fall. I avoid it because I simply cannot face the sheer, monumental effort of it. The thought of walking down those bright, fluorescent-lit aisles, trying to focus enough to decide between three different brands of low-sodium chicken broth, standing in the checkout line and having to smile and make small talk with the cashier about the weather... it just feels completely impossible. My brain is too full of worry to process anything else. 

It's the same with the yard work. I've always taken a great deal of pride in my lawn. I have this wonderful Honda push mower, self-propelled, dual blades, really chops the clippings fine so they mulch right back into the soil, leaves the grass looking like a professional golf course. I usually mow every Thursday morning without fail. But the grass is getting quite high now, and the dandelions are absolutely taking over the front beds. I look out the window at it, and I know I should go out to the shed and pull the mower out, check the oil, fill the gas tank... but I just feel that heavy weight in my chest, and I turn away. 

And again, I'm not avoiding the yard because it reminds me of her condition. The fall happened over by the garage on the concrete, not on the grass anyway. I'm just avoiding the task because I have absolutely zero energy or mental capacity to do it. All my energy is being burned up just sitting in that kitchen chair, terrified that I'm going to mess up her care. So, no, I'm not running from reminders. I'm just completely running on empty.
Are there any activities that you used to enjoy before your wife's fall that you have tried to do since then but found you couldn't bring yourself to do?

Well, yes, as I touched on a few minutes ago, there’s that alumni mentoring program. I really used to get so much joy out of that. I have my master's degree in public administration, you see, and for the last ten years, I've just loved—I mean, really looked forward to—connecting with these bright-eyed graduates. I'd usually meet them for coffee downtown at this little place called The Roasted Bean, or we'd do a video call, and I'd get such a thrill out of helping them polish their resumes or prep for their first big interviews. 

Just last week, I actually tried. I sat down at my desk, booted up the computer, and opened the email link for a scheduled call with a young woman who was looking to get into non-profit management. I had her file right in front of me. But I just... I stared at the screen. I couldn't bring myself to click the button to join the meeting. My chest got tight, and I ended up just shutting the laptop completely. I’ve completely stopped showing up for those mentoring sessions now. 

And it's the exact same story with my other community commitments. I've been on the board of the local Historical Society for years—like I said, I'm a massive Civil War buff—and we were right in the middle of planning our annual summer fundraiser. I used to love organizing the silent auction for that, calling up local businesses, putting together the gift baskets with the cellophane and the ribbons... it was fun for me! But I haven't gone to a single meeting since the accident. They call, they leave voicemails asking for my input on the catering, and I just sit there and listen to the machine record their voices. 

But honestly, doctor, it doesn't even stop at the things I used to enjoy. That's the terrifying part. It’s bleeding into absolutely everything. Things I used to handle without even thinking twice—just the automatic parts of life—are now slipping badly. I know I mentioned the bills piling up earlier, but you have to understand, I used to have this meticulous filing system. I paid everything the day the mail arrived, balanced the checkbook down to the exact penny every Sunday evening. Now, I'm seeing pink envelopes with "Final Notice" printed on them sitting right next to the napkin holder, and I can't bring myself to open them. 

The home upkeep, the basic household routines... it's all just falling apart. I told you about the lawn and the vacuuming, but even something as simple as taking the trash out on Tuesday nights. I know the bin is overflowing. I know the sanitation truck comes at 6 AM sharp on Wednesday morning, they're always very punctual in our neighborhood. I can look right at the garbage can, knowing all I have to do is tie the plastic bag and walk it down the driveway, but I just... I can't do it. I just turn around and go back to my chair. I can't seem to participate in my own life anymore.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep since your wife's fall?

Sleep? Well... you know, honestly, no, I wouldn't say my sleep has changed. Which I suppose might sound a bit surprising, given everything I've just been telling you about how completely overwhelmed I am. But... well, we have this absolutely wonderful Stearns & Foster mattress. We bought it about five years ago, maybe six now, at the Macy's over at the mall during one of their big Labor Day sales. It's a firm mattress but it has this plush pillow top, very supportive for the lower back, which is so important at our age. 

And my routine hasn't really shifted. I usually help my wife get settled for the night, make sure her water pitcher is full and her little call bell is right there on the nightstand next to her reading glasses, and then I get into bed around 10:30 PM. We always watch the Channel 4 local news first—we've been watching David and Sarah anchor that broadcast for at least a decade, they have such a nice rapport, very professional—and then it's lights out. 

And the truth is, doctor, once my head hits that pillow, I am just out cold. I sleep right through until about 6:00 AM, just like I always have before the accident. I think... I think it's because I am just so profoundly, deeply exhausted by the time the day is over. Not physically exhausted, you understand, because as I said, I'm barely doing anything around the house, the mower is just sitting in the shed. But mentally. The sheer mental toll of sitting there, agonizing over her care, terrified that I'm failing her, watching the mail pile up... it drains every single ounce of energy I have. 

So by the time 10:30 rolls around, my brain just completely shuts down. It's like a computer pulling the plug. So no, I haven't noticed any tossing and turning or waking up in the middle of the night or anything like that. Honestly, sleep is the only time I get any actual relief from this constant, gnawing dread. It's the waking up and having to face the reality of my complete inability to function... that's the real nightmare.
Do you consistently feel worthless or guilty about your situation and inability to care for your wife?

Guilty? Worthless? No... no, I wouldn't use those words at all, doctor. I mean, I certainly don't feel worthless. I know I have value. I've been a good provider, a loving husband to my wife for forty-two years now. We actually celebrated our ruby anniversary just a couple of years ago with a lovely trip up to coastal Maine, stayed in this beautiful little bed and breakfast in Kennebunkport, right on the water, ate lobster rolls every day... we had such a wonderful time. I know my worth as a person and as a partner. I spent thirty years managing budgets and personnel for the county, so I know I'm a capable, intelligent man. 

And as for feeling guilty about my inability to care for her right now... I don't think guilt is the right word either. It's not that I'm choosing not to care for her out of selfishness, which I suppose is what would cause guilt. I *want* to care for her, desperately. I want to be the one who handles everything perfectly. But when I look at that color-coded medication schedule the discharge nurse gave us—the blood thinners at this hour, the pain management at that hour, the specific ways I'm supposed to help her pivot from the chair to the walker so she doesn't put weight on the wrong joint—it's not guilt I feel. It's just absolute, unadulterated terror. 

I don't sit in that kitchen chair thinking, 'I'm a worthless person.' I sit there thinking, 'This is entirely too much, this is completely beyond my training, and if I make one wrong move, I could put her right back in the hospital.' I feel completely out of my depth, like I've been dropped into the middle of the ocean without a life vest. So, no, I'm not beating myself up with guilt or feeling like I have no worth. I just feel completely paralyzed by the sheer, monumental responsibility of it all. It's just... it's just short-circuited my entire system.
Are there things you used to do before your wife's fall that you can't seem to start or finish now?

Well, yes, doctor, and I suppose this goes right back to what I was trying to explain just a few minutes ago. It's exactly like I was saying—it really applies to just about every single task you can think of, whether it's something I used to do for fun or just a chore. 

As I mentioned earlier, I’ve completely stopped showing up for my mentoring sessions with those young graduates, and all my other community commitments, like the Historical Society board... I just can't even start them. I literally can't bring myself to click the link to start a video meeting, or pick up the phone to return a voicemail about the summer fundraiser. I just sit there.

But it's the everyday stuff, too, which is what really frightens me. The things I used to handle without even thinking—just the automatic parts of running a home—they are all slipping so badly now. I can't seem to start or finish any of it. Like I was saying about the bills... I used to have that whole meticulous filing system, paying everything the day it arrived, balancing the checkbook on Sunday evenings, and now I just stare at those pink final notices sitting by the napkin holder and I can't even begin the process of opening the envelopes. 

And the home upkeep, the basic household routines... it's the exact same story. Whether it's the vacuuming, or the lawn mower just sitting out there in the shed, or even just taking the trash down to the curb for the Wednesday morning pickup like I described. I know exactly what needs to be done, I know all the steps to finish the job, but I just... I completely freeze up. I can't start the tasks, and I certainly can't finish them. Everything is just grinding to an absolute halt.
Do you feel like you're a burden to your wife or others around you?

A burden? Well... no, I wouldn't say I feel like a burden, doctor. Not in the sense that I'm requiring other people to take care of me, or that I'm actively dragging anyone down. It's... it's quite the opposite, really. I'm the one who is supposed to be doing the burden-carrying right now. 

My wife, she's the one who had the terrible fall, she's the one with the shattered hip and the pins and the grueling physical therapy schedule. She's the one who needs help getting to the bathroom in the middle of the night and needs someone to make sure her compression socks are put on correctly so she doesn't get a blood clot. She needs me. I'm supposed to be her rock, her caregiver. 

And as for our daughter, Emily... she lives three states away, in Ohio, near Cleveland. She has her own life, her own career—she's a middle school principal, which is incredibly demanding, dealing with parents and teachers and budgets all day long. She has three teenagers of her own. I would absolutely never call her up and ask her to drop everything to come down here and manage our household just because her father can't seem to figure out how to open a piece of mail or sort out a medication schedule. 

So, no, I don't feel like a burden because I'm not asking anyone for help. I'm not leaning on anyone. I'm just... I'm just sitting here, completely failing at being the person who is supposed to be carrying the load. I know I'm letting my wife down by being so paralyzed, but I'm not burdening her with my problems. I try very hard to keep all this dread and anxiety to myself when I'm in the room with her. I just put on a brave face, plump her pillows, and then I go back out to the kitchen table and stare at the wall. So, no, "burden" isn't the word I'd use. It's more of a profound, isolating sense of inadequacy.
Do you feel like you're a bad person because you can't take care of your wife the way you want to?

A bad person? No, doctor, no... I don't feel like a bad person. I really don't. I mean, I know what a bad person looks like. A bad person is someone who intentionally causes harm, someone who acts out of malice or selfishness. A bad person would look at their wife of forty-two years, lying there in a hospital bed in the living room, and just walk out the front door because it was too inconvenient. That's not me. That will never be me. 

I'm not a bad person, I'm just... I'm a terrified person. I'm a person who is completely overwhelmed. You see, when I was managing the county budgets, if I made a mistake, well, maybe some funds got misallocated, maybe a project got delayed, but nobody got hurt. Nobody's physical well-being was on the line. But here... if I mess up her medication, if I misread that tiny, impossible print on the prescription bottle and give her too much of the blood thinner, or if I don't support her exactly right when she's trying to use the commode and she falls again... the consequences are just catastrophic. 

So, when I sit there, unable to move, unable to just get up and do the things I know I need to do for her, it's not because there's some darkness or badness in my soul. It's because the fear of doing it wrong is so immense, so heavy, that it just crushes me flat. I want to be the perfect caregiver. I want to make her comfortable and safe. The desire is there, the love is absolutely there, just as strong as the day we got married. It's just the execution... the ability to push past this wall of panic... that's what's failing me. Not my morality. Not my character. Just my nerves, I suppose. So, no, I don't think I'm a bad person at all. Just a very, very frightened one who is failing at the most important job he's ever had.
Are there any activities that you used to enjoy before your wife's fall that you've completely lost interest in now?

Lost interest? No, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest at all, doctor. That’s a very specific word, "interest," and I think it’s incredibly important to distinguish between not being interested in something and just... well, not being able to actually do it, which is what we were just talking about. 

Take my reading, for example. I’ve always been a voracious reader, particularly of American history—specifically the post-Civil War Reconstruction era, which is a fascinating period if you really delve into the local municipal records. I suppose some people might handle it better, yes. Maybe if I had a medical background, if I had been a nurse or an EMT instead of a county budget manager, I would just step right into the role. I'd be checking the charts, adjusting the pillows, managing the physical therapy schedules without missing a single beat. Maybe it is. Maybe I should be much stronger. I look at my neighbor, Sarah—the one who brought the baked ziti I mentioned earlier—and when her husband had his bypass surgery last year, she seemed so incredibly put together. She was out there mowing the front lawn, for heaven's sake, while he was inside recovering! She just handled it. But then again, a bypass is a scheduled procedure, mostly. You have time to prepare, to get the house ready, to mentally brace yourself. This was so sudden. One minute she was just reaching for the good china in the top cabinet—which, I have told her a hundred times to let me get for her, I even bought this very sturdy step stool with a handrail from the hardware store specifically for that cabinet, but she insisted she didn't need it—and the very next minute, there was this awful sound, and our whole lives were just completely upended. 

So, I don't know if my reaction is out of proportion. I don't have a baseline for this kind of terror. I've never been tested like this before. I know the bin is overflowing. I know the sanitation truck comes at 6 AM sharp on Wednesday morning, they're always very punctual in our neighborhood. I can look right at the garbage can, knowing all I have to do is tie the plastic bag and walk it down the driveway, but I just... I can't do it. I just turn around and go back to my chair. The sheer mental toll of sitting there, agonizing over her care, terrified that I'm failing her, watching the mail pile up... it drains every single ounce of energy I have.

So no, I haven't noticed any tossing and turning or waking up in the middle of the night or anything like that. I feel completely out of my depth, like I've been dropped into the middle of the ocean without a life vest. So, no, I'm not beating myself up with guilt or feeling like I have no worth. Disproportionate? Well... I don't know, doctor.
